1.pericope_label: Keep not thou silence, O God: hold not thy peace, and be not still, O God... Come, and let us cut them off from being a nation; that the name of Israel may be no more in remembrance

schools.summary: Divides between philology and history. One line notes that the opening runs literally God, not silence to thee, that the enemies' tumult is a roaring like the sea, and that their crafty counsel is a plot made crafty; the hidden ones are those under God's close protection. The other places the psalm historically, observing that it closes the twelve Asaph psalms and canvassing a case for the Maccabean age, where sudden hostility on every side against a newly independent people is judged to fit far better than opposition to the rebuilding of Jerusalem.

Reads the psalm as the church's prayer under threat of extinction, referred to the confederacy that came against Jehoshaphat and matched against the chronicler's roll of nations. The doubled opening plea is taken as urgency confessed: patience under delay is a duty, but God in condescension permits his people to beg him to hurry. God's silence is defined as his not answering prayer, not pleading their cause, not rebuking their enemies.

Supplies the historical and geographical frame: the invaders already in Judea and encamped by the Dead Sea, eight or ten nations bound in one purpose to leave no record of Israel, the plot so secret that the king heard nothing until his territory was overrun. On the hidden ones it canvasses the versions, which give thy holy ones, thy saints and the hidden things in thy treasures, and allows that the temple, the ark and its stores may be meant rather than the people.

Draws out the silence as a picture: God seeming to observe an exact neutrality, sitting by as a man astonished or a mighty man that cannot save, with the comfort that his speaking is his acting. Notes that a prayer offered in great distress is still called a song. Presses the appeal to the Mighty One rather than to any human force, and hears in the enemies a hungry pack all giving tongue at once, already shouting over the feast.

Reads the title as the psalm's key. Asaph means congregation, in Greek synagogue, so the name stands for the assembled people of God; and the opening question is taken of Christ, reckoned in his humiliation comparable to other men, even to the robbers crucified beside him, but incomparable when he comes in glory.

debates.question: What crisis does the psalm answer to?

positions.summary: The confederacy against Jehoshaphat, on the strength of the matching roll of nations and the prophet of Asaph's line who foretold the overthrow.
The Maccabean age, where hostility breaking out on every side against a newly independent people fits the psalm better than the obstruction of the rebuilding of Jerusalem.
No datable crisis: the title is read spiritually, the congregation speaking and the question addressed to Christ.

debates.question: Who or what are the hidden ones the enemies consult against?

positions.summary: The people of Israel, God's peculiar treasure under his close protection.
Possibly not the people at all, but the temple, the ark and the treasures stored there.

outliers.reading: Treats the title as a doorway to be read before entering, taking at the end to mean Christ and identifying the people put far off by way of the inscription set over the cross in three tongues.

themes: Keep not thou silence, O God: hold not thy peace, and be not still, O God.
For, lo, thine enemies make a tumult: and they that hate thee have lifted up the head.
They have taken crafty counsel against thy people, and consulted against thy hidden ones.
They have said, Come, and let us cut them off from being a nation; that the name of Israel may be no more in remembrance.

5.pericope_label: For they have consulted together with one consent: they are confederate against thee... Make their nobles like Oreb, and like Zeeb: yea, all their princes as Zebah, and as Zalmunna

schools.summary: Unsettles the roll of nations from the text side. The confederacy is literally a cut covenant; Gebal, if a noun, must be a synonym for Edom, but is more likely a verb, so that the line reads Ammon and Amalek are joined together, the Philistines with the men of Tyre; the final name may be Syria under the grander old title rather than Assyria proper; and the claimed possession is pastures rather than houses. Alongside this the historical line supplies the mechanism of the old victory, the Kishon carrying off the corpses and En-dor lying within the battlefield.

Notes that men who agree in nothing else agree in opposing the people of God, places Gebal in Phoenicia near Tyre, and reports and rejects a reading that would date the war after Hezekiah. On the precedents it identifies the princes named and keeps the two old routs distinct.

Carries the geography and the antiquarian detail: the covenant rite of the divided victim, the tents that mark migratory peoples, the Hagarenes east of Gilead, the Giblites as unconquered stone-squarers who worked on the temple, the Philistines as former tributaries who turned when it suited, Tyre joining in hope of mainland territory. On the precedents it supplies the fate of each named chief. A second voice in this school places Gebal instead among Arabian peoples on the southern edge of Canaan.

Reads the confederacy genealogically — Edom nearest of kin yet first in enmity, the Ishmaelites keeping up the old grudge, Moab a kinsman born of incest — and treats the prayer as prophecy binding on all later enemies of the church, grounded on the unchangeableness of God. Presses the precedent hard: a brook can be as deadly as a sea when God wills it, and those who would not give Israel a place above ground were denied a hiding place under it.

debates.question: What is Gebal in the roll of nations?

positions.summary: The Phoenician city near Tyre, whose people were the Giblites — unconquered Canaanite stone-squarers.
An Arabian people on the southern border of Canaan, where most of the confederacy lived.
Probably not a proper name at all, but a verb, so that the clause states that Ammon and Amalek are joined together.

debates.question: Which defeat does the reference to En-dor recall?

positions.summary: Gideon's rout of Midian in the valley of Jezreel, near which En-dor lay.
The destruction of Jabin and Sisera, whose battlefield included the place.
Neither straightforwardly: the account of that battle never names En-dor at all.

outliers.reading: Proposes reading one name in the confederacy as a verb rather than a proper noun, which would remove a nation from the roll altogether and redistribute the clause among its neighbours.

themes: For they have consulted together with one consent: they are confederate against thee:
The tabernacles of Edom, and the Ishmaelites; of Moab, and the Hagarenes;
Gebal, and Ammon, and Amalek; the Philistines with the inhabitants of Tyre;
Assur also is joined with them: they have holpen the children of Lot. Selah.
Do unto them as unto the Midianites; as to Sisera, as to Jabin, at the brook of Kison:
Which perished at En–dor: they became as dung for the earth.
Make their nobles like Oreb, and like Zeeb: yea, all their princes as Zebah, and as Zalmunna:
Who said, Let us take to ourselves the houses of God in possession.

13.pericope_label: O my God, make them like a wheel; as the stubble before the wind... That men may know that thou, whose name alone is JEHOVAH, art the most high over all the earth

schools.summary: Presses the botany and the theology of the closing wish. The word for wheel is shown to be rendered elsewhere as a rolling thing, with thistledown in the margin and dust of a wheel in the Greek, and is identified with a wild plant whose globes break loose and are driven before the wind. The name at the close is read as thy name, which is Jehovah, so that the nations seek him not merely as God but as the God of Israel, and the aim of the whole imprecation is that the enemies lay hold of mercy in the middle of their downfall, the knowing at the end not limited to a bare perception of the punishment's justice.

Takes the wheel as a rolling thing driven before the wind rather than an instrument, notes how swiftly a kindled forest goes, and glosses the shame as disappointment rather than penitence, recording a rendering that would fill their faces with fire. On the closing name it reads being, eternity and unchangeableness, excluding not the Son or the Spirit but every fictitious deity.

Commits to the threshing floor throughout: the broad wheel rolled over the grain, the chaff carried off against the wind, and even the burning mountains explained as chaff fired on the hilltop floors. Then defends the imprecations directly, setting them against the ancient custom of cursing an enemy before battle and insisting they touch only the present attempt, not the enemies' souls or eternal state. A second voice in the school keeps the wheel simply as instability and confines the burning mountains to their woods.

Reads the images morally. The wheel means hearts unfixed, in contrast to the fixed hearts of those who trust God; driven stubble must not only be driven but burnt; the storm raises terror in the sinner's own heart, so that the proudest defier can be made afraid as a grasshopper. On the purpose of the curses the school divides between seeking the enemies' repentance and, where they remain obstinate, invoking justice to carry the sentence out.

debates.question: What is the wheel the enemies are to be made like?

positions.summary: A rolling plant driven before the wind — thistledown, or the globes of a wild artichoke broken loose from the stem.
The threshing wheel rolled over grain, so that the figure is of being crushed and winnowed.
Simply instability: men who counted on a sure possession made unfixed and easily removed.

debates.question: Do the closing imprecations aim at the enemies' conversion or their destruction?

positions.summary: Conversion: no confusion is to be desired for them but such as may be a step towards repentance.
Conversion, and more — they are to lay hold of mercy in the middle of their ruin, the final knowing including knowledge unto salvation.
Conversion where shame works, but destruction where it does not: better they perished than that Israel be rooted up.

outliers.reading: Breaks off to defend the psalm's curses against the objection that they are unchristian, arguing from a contemporary analogy of invasion that he would offer every one of them himself, while restricting their reach to the enemies' present attempt.

themes: O my God, make them like a wheel; as the stubble before the wind.
As the fire burneth a wood, and as the flame setteth the mountains on fire;
So persecute them with thy tempest, and make them afraid with thy storm.
Fill their faces with shame; that they may seek thy name, O Lord.
Let them be confounded and troubled for ever; yea, let them be put to shame, and perish:
That men may know that thou, whose name alone is Jehovah, art the most high over all the earth.
